summary: Learners plot bivariate data as a scatter graph on labelled, consistently-scaled axes, describe the correlation, and, where there is a correlation, draw a single straight line of best fit by eye (balanced with points roughly equal either side, not a dot-to-dot join and not forced through the origin). They use it to estimate within the data range (interpolation) while treating predictions beyond the data (extrapolation) with caution. The discriminating skill is constructing and balancing the line, and knowing where it is safe to read from.
misconceptions: Joining the points dot-to-dot instead of drawing a single straight trend line
Drawing a line of best fit that is unbalanced (most points on one side) or forcing it through the origin
Extrapolating beyond the data range and treating the prediction as reliable
Plotting on an inconsistent/non-linear scale, leaving axes unlabelled, or swapping the x- and y-values

activities.title: Plot and balance a line of best fit
steps: Take a table of paired measurements (e.g. 10 pupils' height and arm-span) and plot each pair as one cross on a two-axis grid.
Label both axes with the variable names and choose a consistent, linear scale; where the data does not start near zero, use an axis break rather than distorting the scale.

First judge the direction of the correlation from the overall pattern (if there is no correlation, do not draw a line). Then draw a SINGLE straight trend line in that direction and adjust it (tilt and shift) until roughly equal numbers of points sit above and below along its whole length.
Deliberately draw a wrong dot-to-dot zig-zag joining consecutive points alongside the correct line, and explain in words why the single trend line, not the join, summarises the whole cloud.
State the correlation type (positive, negative, or none) from the overall pattern.
activities.insight: The line of best fit is one straight summary of the whole point cloud, positioned so points balance either side - it is not a path connecting consecutive points and is not required to pass through the origin.

activities.title: Interpolate inside, question outside
steps: On a scatter with a correct line of best fit, mark the data range on the x-axis (the lowest to highest observed value).
Read off an estimated y-value for an x inside the range (e.g. predicted score for 5 hours' revision when the data runs 1-8 hours), and state it as a reasonable estimate.
Attempt a prediction well beyond the data (e.g. 20 hours) and explain why that value is unreliable because the trend is not known to continue.
Note that interpolated estimates are more trustworthy when the correlation is strong, and keep every read-off tied to its context so the number means something.
activities.insight: Estimating within the observed data range is reasonable (especially with a strong correlation), but extending the line beyond the data gives an unreliable prediction because the trend may not continue.

activities.title: Check reading and choice (scorable practice)
steps: Given a scatter with a line already drawn, describe the correlation and read an interpolated value.
Choose the correct line of best fit from options that include a dot-to-dot join, an unbalanced line, and a well-balanced line, and justify the choice.
Decide whether a far-outside prediction is reliable and explain why not.
Place a line of best fit onto a given scatter (accepting a small range of acceptable positions).
activities.insight: Being able to recognise a good line and read inside the range confirms understanding, but it does not by itself demonstrate the ability to construct and balance a line from raw data.

activities.title: Annotated reference scatter
steps: Study a worked scatter whose axes, correlation type, balanced line of best fit, and interpolation vs extrapolation zones are labelled.
Reveal and read each annotation: what each axis shows, why the line balances the cloud, and where reliable reading ends.
activities.insight: A labelled example clarifies the vocabulary and the target of a good line, serving as a reference before the learner constructs their own.

checkQuestion: Two moves. FIRST, interpret a given representation: 'Here is a scatter graph of hours revised against test score, with a line of best fit already drawn. Describe the correlation, and use the line to estimate the score for someone who revised 5 hours (the data runs from 1 to 8 hours).' THEN, translate/construct: 'Here is a table of 10 pupils' (height, arm-span) measurements. Plot the scatter graph — label the axes and choose a sensible scale — then draw a line of best fit by eye.' Watch the plotting, the scale, and especially how the line is drawn — that construction step is the discriminator.
checkAnswer: Interpretation: names the correlation (e.g. positive) and reads a value from the line WITHIN the data range (interpolation at 5 hours). Construction: plots each pair accurately on axes labelled with the two variables and a consistent scale (an axis break is acceptable), then draws a SINGLE straight trend line in the direction of the correlation with points balanced roughly equally either side — not a dot-to-dot join and not forced through the origin. Drawing one balanced straight line, and reading only within the data range, are the discriminating moves.
